title: Working with the Mills Brothers and the Coquille, Oregon story
summary: He backed the Mills Brothers in the East and in Oregon, where the Mills Brothers' mocking autograph jokes recall a Tulsa union dispute.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Another thing that was good was this like the Red Caps--do you remember when they were hot?
Damita Jo.
And the Mills Brothers. I played with the Mills Brothers.

I'll tell you a coincidence with the Mills Brothers; I worked with them several times so when I was on the west coast there I turned short a lot--I mean to be frank, I didn't have as big a class music like I had a lot of times, but I was satisfying Mr. Public.
I had worked with the Mills Brothers several times back east and in Chicago and there was this number that I think Cab Calloway did--Sabre Dance--well, I had a Parker

Berry arrangement--oh, it was terrific and we had figured out a deal that just before they pull the curtain, we had the sabres in front of the stands and the lights and we did that show one time with the Mills Brothers. We took as many bows as the Mills Brothers.

So I was going up the west coast once, I think it was Coquille, Oregon, and sometimes these towns will try to bring in big things and so they had contacted the Mills Brothers for a dance, and so the Mills Brothers told them, well apparently the man gave two prices; if it's just the Mills Brothers or if we had to bring a back up band it's got to be so and so. So the guy told them, this gig that I want you for, we're making that a big affair, we have Ernie Fields in there. And so they told him, enough said.
They came into this town and they were in town, they notified us time for rehearsal, work out all them G sharps and this and that and everything, and brother, we had a time.

We finally kind of made it and we played the show, but I could mention this, this deal I was telling you about, the union thing that happened in Tulsa, well, this same band that they were having trouble about, the guy finally paid them but he had to get some more musicians and this man was angry (inaudible). So anyway, when I went out to my business agent, why did you let him put this on me and so and so, kidding he said, well, I don't know; and he had some pictures on the desk. I said let me have one of them pictures there and they guy said yes, autograph it and say, remember Coquille, Oregon. I said you better not, I'll shoot you, and he fell out.
That's the Mills Brothers?
Yeah, Mills Brothers. They said no, we're not going to do that, we'll say Chicago. I said that will be all right. So they said, one thing Ernie, you ought to have a (inaudible); In Coquille

you finally cleared it, but what they had up here with us, when we called a number, they never heard of it and they couldn't play it and they couldn't read and they said it was really murder but in Coquille you finally made it.
So you were the business agent, you went out to the club to collect the (inaudible)?
Yeah.
What was the name of the club?
Ziegfelds.
And the Mills Brothers came in all these years later and played?
Yeah; just last year.
Last year?
Yeah.
They remembered?
They remembered, they remembered when the man told them who it was, because we were so terrific all along in those theatres and they said forget about it.
(Inaudible). No, you couldn't but I continued going out and had all those dances there; they had to pay them too, they were under the musicians, but after all it cost and everything.
